1
Introduction

Welcome to momentum

momentum is a goal-setting, reflection, recognition and leadership support platform, designed to be integrated into an organization’s existing intranet. It helps employees take ownership of their development, notice their own progress and reflect on what helps or gets in the way. It gives leaders a better basis for individual support, and it helps everyone see how their work connects to what colleagues in other departments are doing.

The application works at three levels. At the individual level, employees set one monthly goal and two weekly goals, plan with WOOP and reflect every Friday. At the interpersonal level, leaders use these insights for supportive conversations and colleagues cheer each other on with Bravo!. At the organizational level, monthly updates from each department and the CEO make collective contributions visible.

momentum is

  • A personal space for meaningful goals and reflection
  • A starting point for supportive conversations with your leader
  • A simple way to acknowledge each other’s progress
  • A window into how departments contribute to a shared purpose

momentum is not

  • A performance management or appraisal system
  • A productivity tracker or a tool for surveillance
  • A competition, leaderboard or popularity measure
  • A replacement for everyday conversations and feedback

The principles behind every feature

Progress, not perfection. Support, not comparison. Ownership, not obligation. Support, not evaluation. Learning and development, not merely goal attainment. You will find these principles in how the features are built – colleagues never see what your goals are about, no one sees how many Bravo! anyone receives, and history charts compare people only with themselves – and in how this manual recommends using them.

Your goals, your progress, our shared momentum.

How to read this manual

The manual walks through the application role by role. Features shared by all roles are described once, in sections 2 and 3. Because momentum is currently a demonstration prototype, the manual marks clearly what you are looking at:

In the demo

Implemented and working in the current prototype at orgmomentum.no.

Intended practice

How the organization is meant to use a feature. Guidance, not something the software enforces.

Future development

Would require further development before a real organizational implementation.

momentum also has two built-in guides. The Info tab explains purpose, privacy, good goals and WOOP to everyone, and the Leader Handbook develops leaders’ motivational leadership. This manual explains the application itself and points you to those resources where they go deeper.

2
First steps

Getting started

Opening momentum

The prototype runs in any modern browser on desktop, tablet or phone. There is nothing to install and no account to create.

  1. Go to orgmomentum.no in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox.
  2. You start as Kari, Product Manager, on the employee Dashboard.
  3. Explore freely. Everything you change is saved in your own browser, so you can close the tab and come back to it later on the same device.

On a desktop, the navigation tabs sit in the header at the top. On narrower screens (tablets in portrait and phones), the tabs move to a navigation bar at the bottom of the screen, within easy reach of your thumb.

The demonstration environment

The prototype contains a fictional technology company that is improving its customer onboarding experience. It has 22 employees in four departments, each with demonstration goals, reflections and history:

DepartmentLeaderEmployees
ProductMartin, Head of Product7 (including Kari)
DesignNora, Head of Design5
EngineeringErik, Head of Engineering6
People & CultureCamilla, Head of People & Culture4
What the prototype is – and is not

momentum is currently a functional demonstration built as one self-contained web page. There is no login, no server and no real employee data. Your changes are stored only in your own browser (using its local storage), they do not synchronize between browsers, devices or visitors, and there are no real push notifications. Week and month labels follow your device’s date. Do not enter real or confidential information.

The three roles

You can view momentum from three perspectives without separate accounts or passwords. Each role sees different features and different information.

Employee

Kari, Product Manager. Sets goals, writes reflections, sends Bravo!.

Dashboard · Team · Organization · Info

Leader

Martin, Head of Product. Sees his department’s goals and reflections, writes department updates.

Dashboard · Team · Organization · Info

CEO

Hanne, CEO. Sees aggregated organization and department insights, writes CEO updates.

Dashboard · Organization · Info

Switching between roles

The first time you open momentum, a gold hint reading Try the different roles! points to the avatar in the upper-right corner. Selecting the hint opens the menu with the role switcher highlighted; the × closes it. The hint disappears once you have closed it or opened the avatar menu, and it comes back after you reset the demo data.

  1. Select your avatar in the upper-right corner.
  2. Under Demo · view as, choose Employee, Leader or CEO.
  3. momentum opens that person’s Dashboard. A short message confirms who you are now viewing as, and the label next to the bell (for example Demo · Leader) reminds you on desktop.
Try thisTick off one of Kari’s weekly goals as an employee, then switch to Leader and open Kari’s card. You will see the same goal from Martin’s side – and the CEO will only ever see it as part of a count.

Role switching exists only because this is a demo. In a real implementation, each person would sign in with their own account and see only their own role Future development.

Resetting the demo data

To start over, open the avatar menu and select Reset demo data. momentum restores the original demonstration state immediately.

Reset cannot be undoneThere is no confirmation step. Resetting removes everything you have entered in this browser: goals, reflections, WOOP plans, 1:1 notes, drafts and published updates, avatar changes, Info edits and your Leadership Reflection Tool entries. Copy anything you want to keep first.
3
Common features

Navigating momentum

The header

The deep aubergine header is the same in every role. From left to right, it contains the momentum logo and name, the navigation tabs, a label showing the current demo role, the notification bell and your avatar. The selected tab is marked with a gold underline.

TabWhat you find thereAvailable to
DashboardYour personal space. Employees set goals and reflect; leaders see their department; the CEO sees the organization.All roles
TeamA feed of achievements in your own department, where you can send Bravo!.Employee, Leader
OrganizationMonthly updates from each department and the CEO.All roles
InfoAbout momentum, privacy, tips for good goals, WOOP and FAQ. Leaders also find the Leader Handbook here.All roles

Notifications

The bell shows a gold badge with the number of unread notifications. Select it to open the notification panel, where notifications are grouped into Today, This week and Earlier. Unread items have a light purple background.

You may be notified when:

  • someone sends you a Bravo!
  • a teammate achieves a goal – you can send a Bravo! straight from the notification
  • a department or the CEO publishes a monthly update
  • it is time to set your weekly goals, or a weekly summary is ready

Selecting a notification marks it as read and takes you to the right place: an achievement opens the Team feed, an update opens Organization with the post expanded. Mark all as read clears the badge. Close the panel by selecting the bell again, clicking elsewhere or pressing Esc.

Notifications are there to support meaningful engagement, not to make you check the app constantly Intended practice. In the demo they appear only inside the application; there are no push or email notifications Future development.

Your avatar and profile

The avatar menu shows your name, title and department, and gives access to Edit avatar, Demo · view as and Reset demo data.

Instead of uploading a photo, everyone designs an avatar. This keeps the interface friendly and lets people choose how they are represented. Your avatar is what colleagues see in the Team feed, notifications and updates.

  1. Open the avatar menu and select Edit avatar. Employees can also use the Edit avatar button on the Dashboard, or select their large avatar there.
  2. Choose a style: Character or Initials.
  3. Pick a background colour. For a character, also choose skin tone, hair (none, short, long, bun or curly), hair colour, eyes, mouth, an accessory (glasses, sunglasses or a cap) and the colour of the top.
  4. Not sure? Select Randomize for a new combination.
  5. Select Save, or Cancel to keep your current avatar.
4
Kari’s view

Employee perspective

The employee Dashboard is your personal space for setting goals, following your progress and reflecting on your working week. Everything on it belongs to you: you decide what your goals are, how you describe your week and when something feels done.

The Dashboard at a glance

At the top, a greeting shows the current week and month, together with two chips: how many of your weekly goals you have achieved (for example Weekly goals: 1 of 2 achieved) and the current stage of your monthly goal. Below are three cards, in the order you will typically use them during a week:

  1. Weekly goals – two goals for this week.
  2. Friday reflection – how did your week go?
  3. Monthly goal and WOOP – what you want to learn or get better at this month, and a plan for getting there.

Goal texts and WOOP answers are saved automatically as you type. A line at the bottom of the page reminds you who can see what.

Setting and completing weekly goals

At the start of each week, set two self-selected goals. They can be small steps towards your monthly goal, or concern something else that matters in your work – learning, collaboration, asking for feedback or finishing a piece of work. There is no expectation that every weekly goal supports the monthly goal.

  1. Write your goal in the field for Weekly goal 1, then Weekly goal 2.
  2. If a goal is a step towards your monthly goal, select + Link to monthly goal. The goal is then tagged Supports monthly goal. Select the tag again to remove the link.
  3. When you have achieved a goal, select the round check button. The goal turns green and the progress dots fill in.
  4. Ticked it by mistake, or not quite done after all? Select the check button again to reopen the goal. There is no rush and no score.

When you achieve a goal, your colleagues in the Team feed see that you reached Weekly goal 1 or Weekly goal 2 – never what the goal was about. In the demo, a simulated colleague may send you a Bravo! a few seconds later to show how this works.

Good weekly goals are…

  • meaningful to you and your work
  • specific enough that you know when they are done
  • challenging, yet realistic for the week ahead
  • within a reasonable degree of your own control

For example

  • Lead one customer interview with Silje observing
  • Give Jonas feedback on his funnel analysis
  • Practise the presentation and ask a colleague for feedback
  • Try a new working method on an ongoing task
Weekly goals give direction and make progress tangible, but they are only a small part of your work. Never pursue them at the expense of quality, ethics, collaboration, your well-being or other responsibilities – and the number of goals you complete says nothing about your productivity or performance Intended practice. More tips in Info → Tips for Good Goals.

Writing your Friday reflection

At the end of the week, take a few minutes to look back. The card asks one open question – How did your week go? – and offers some questions for inspiration: What did you learn? Where did you get to decide for yourself? Who helped you, or who did you help? What got in the way? You do not have to answer them all, or in any particular order. There are deliberately no predefined answer options: write in your own words about what you find relevant.

  1. Write your reflection in the text field.
  2. Select Save reflection. A message confirms that your leader can now read it.
  3. You can keep editing your reflection until the week ends.

Unfinished goals are useful information, not failure. If something outside your control got in the way – too many meetings, unclear priorities, missing tools – the reflection is a good place to say so, because it helps your leader see where they can help.

Your reflection is visible to you and your leader only. Share what you feel comfortable sharing. Reflections are not weekly reports: their length, frequency or degree of positivity should never be evaluated Intended practice.

Setting your monthly goal

At the start of each month, choose one broader goal that answers the question What do you want to learn or get better at this month? It can be more ambitious and development-oriented than a weekly goal: building a skill, growing more confident in an area, improving a way of working or learning something new. Choose something challenging yet attainable – and personally meaningful. No numbers or targets are needed.

Write your goal in the large field on the monthly goal card. Then work through WOOP below it.

Planning with WOOP

WOOP – Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan – is a science-based mental strategy that combines mental contrasting with if–then planning. Rather than only imagining success, you also identify what in you might hold you back and decide in advance how to respond.

StepWhat to do in momentumKari’s example
W · WishFilled in automatically from your monthly goal.Get comfortable leading customer interviews on my own
O · OutcomeImagine the best result of reaching your wish, and why it matters to you.I lead interviews calmly, customers open up, and I feel I really understand what they need.
O · ObstacleName the main obstacle in you: a habit, feeling or thought.I get nervous and over-prepare questions instead of practising out loud.
P · PlanComplete the If and then fields to link the obstacle to an action.If I notice I’m rewriting my interview guide the day before, then I’ll do a ten-minute practice interview with a colleague instead.

Your weekly goals can then become smaller steps, such as “Conduct a practice interview with a colleague and ask for feedback”. Your leader sees WOOP plan ✓ on your card once Outcome, Obstacle and both parts of the Plan are filled in.

Not every obstacle is yours to fixWOOP focuses on internal obstacles. Workload, missing resources or unclear expectations are organizational barriers – raise them in your reflection or with your leader, whose job it is to help remove them. Read more in Info → Using WOOP to Set Your Monthly Goals or at woopmylife.org.

Updating your monthly progress

Under Where are you now?, choose the stage that fits best: Just started, Making progress, Almost there or Achieved. The selected stage appears in the chip at the top of your Dashboard. Selecting Achieved shares that you reached your monthly goal in the Team feed; choosing an earlier stage again reopens the goal. Write your goal before choosing a stage.

Understanding your personal progress overview

The two chips at the top of the Dashboard summarize where you are this week and this month. They are for you – a quick reminder of your own direction, not a score. Your leader also sees how many weekly goals you achieved over the last weeks, compared only with your own earlier weeks and never with colleagues (see section 5).

The Team feed and Bravo!

The Team tab shows achievements in your department, newest first. Each item shows a colleague’s avatar and name, whether they achieved Weekly goal 1, Weekly goal 2 or their monthly goal (marked Monthly), and when. Your own achievements appear as “You achieved…”.

  1. Open the Team tab.
  2. Select Bravo! next to an achievement you would like to acknowledge.
  3. The button changes to Sent, and your colleague receives a notification. You can send one Bravo! per person per achievement.

No one can see how many Bravo! anyone has received, and there are no leaderboards. Bravo! is a voluntary, genuine gesture of encouragement – not a measure of popularity or performance, and there is no expectation to send a certain number or to return one you receive Intended practice. It complements, and does not replace, everyday support between colleagues.

The gold Demo: simulate a teammate button creates an illustrative achievement by a colleague, so you can try sending a Bravo! from the feed or the bell. It exists only in the prototype.
5
Martin’s view

Leader perspective

As a leader, your Dashboard is about the people in your department. It brings together their goals, progress and reflections so you can understand what matters to them, notice where support could help and have better conversations. In the prototype, leaders do not set goals of their own on the Dashboard.

Your goals are yours to pursue. Your leader is there to support you along the way.

The department Dashboard

The page is titled with your department (for example Product team) and has three parts: four overview tiles, an AI summary and a card for each team member.

TileShows
Monthly goals setHow many team members have set a monthly goal
Weekly goals achievedAchieved weekly goals out of all weekly goals set this week
Linked to monthly goalHow many weekly goals are marked as supporting a monthly goal
Reflections writtenHow many team members have saved a Friday reflection

The tiles describe how the team is using momentum and where a conversation might be useful. They are not measures of productivity, motivation or performance.

The AI summary

The dark summary card condenses the week into five parts. The line in the top-right corner shows what the summary is based on.

Overview

Monthly goals set and their stages, how many have completed WOOP, weekly goals achieved compared with last week, how many weekly goals link to monthly goals, and how many reflections were written.

Motivation signals

Possible signals for the three basic psychological needs – autonomy (feeling ownership and choice), competence (feeling effective and growing) and relatedness (feeling connected and supported) – based on words in this week’s reflections. Each need gets one of four labels, with the evidence beside it:

LabelMeaning in the prototype
StrongOnly positive mentions, for example people describing learning or good support
MixedBoth positive and negative mentions
At riskMore negative than positive mentions, for example feeling stuck or alone
No signalsThe need was not mentioned this week

Key obstacles

Themes coded from the reflections, with the number of people mentioning each: Workload & meetings, Unclear priorities, Waiting on others, Tools & resources and Energy & wellbeing.

Who might need a check-in

Up to five team members who might benefit from a conversation, with the reason – for example that they have not set goals yet, feel stuck, want more say or mention low energy.

Suggested actions

Up to five leadership actions linked to what the summary found, such as starting the week with a short priorities check-in, reviewing recurring meetings or offering pairing where people feel stuck.

How to read the AI summary

In the prototype, the summary does not use an AI model. Reflections are coded with simple keyword rules (for example, “meetings” counts as Workload & meetings), and the summary is generated from that coding In the demo. Keywords can easily misread a sentence – “I’m not stuck anymore” still contains “stuck”.

The summary is not a validated assessment of motivation, engagement or mental health. At risk is not a diagnosis, and No signals does not mean a need is unmet. Treat everything as a possible starting point for a conversation: stay curious, consider other explanations and ask for the employee’s own perspective. Suggested actions support your judgement; they do not replace it Intended practice.

Team member cards

Each card shows the person’s name and title, their monthly goal and its stage, whether WOOP is done (WOOP plan ✓ or No WOOP yet), weekly progress and up to three themes coded from their reflection. Green tags are positive need signals, coral tags negative need signals and gold tags obstacles. Select a card, or See details →, to open the individual view.

The individual employee view

Weekly goals

The actual goals, marked Achieved or In progress, and tagged Supports monthly goal where relevant.

Friday reflection

The reflection “in Jonas’s words”, with the automatically coded themes underneath.

Monthly goal

The goal, its stage and the WOOP reflection: outcome, inner obstacle and if–then plan.

Weekly goals achieved

A chart of the last four weeks plus this week, compared only with the employee’s own earlier weeks.

Read the history chart as context, not as evidence of improving or declining performance. Goals differ in difficulty, complexity and relevance from week to week, and a week with fewer ticks may have been a week of more learning.

Notes for your next 1:1

The field Notes for your next 1:1 · only you is your private space to jot down observations, questions or ways you could help. Notes are saved automatically as you type. Within the intended role structure, only you see them. Use them to prepare developmental conversations, never as a hidden performance record Intended practice.

A simple structure for the conversationThe Leader Handbook (chapter 5) suggests four steps: Understand the employee’s perspective, Acknowledge learning and progress, Explore possible next steps together, and Support – agree on what would help, and follow through.

Using insights responsibly

Leaders can see employees’ goals, WOOP and reflections, and employees cannot switch this off. This visibility is deliberate: it lets you offer individual support, constructive feedback and meaningful conversations. It also places a responsibility on you Intended practice.

Do

  • Listen to employees’ perspectives
  • Recognize development and progress, not only results
  • Clarify expectations and priorities
  • Help remove organizational barriers
  • Offer resources, learning opportunities and specific feedback
  • Follow through on the support you offer
  • Treat what people share with discretion

Don’t

  • Monitor productivity through momentum
  • Compare employees by goal attainment
  • Treat reflections as performance evidence
  • Penalize unfinished goals
  • Link goals or engagement to pay, rewards or sanctions
  • Diagnose motivation or well-being from automated signals

You do not need to respond formally to every reflection. Let what you read inform your everyday interactions, follow up when it is relevant, and help employees keep ownership of their goals rather than setting them on their behalf.

Other features for leaders

  • Team feed – the same department feed as employees, where you can send Bravo! (section 4).
  • Organization – read all updates and write your department’s monthly update (section 7).
  • Info – the same guidance employees read, plus the gold Leader Handbook button (sections 8 and 9).
6
Hanne’s view

CEO perspective

The CEO Dashboard gives an aggregated view of the whole organization. It is designed to reveal broader patterns, common barriers and opportunities for support – not to follow individuals. Individual follow-up is the responsibility of each employee’s own leader.

The organizational Dashboard

The page, titled Organization, uses the same four tiles as the leader Dashboard, counted across all employees. Below them, the AI summary This week across the organization contains Overview, Motivation signals, Key obstacles and Suggested actions, plus a Departments at a glance block showing each department’s main obstacle and any needs worth watching. Like the leader summary, it is based on keyword coding in the prototype.

Department cards

Each of the four cards shows the department leader, the number of employees, progress bars for monthly goals set, weekly goals achieved and reflections written, a signal for autonomy, competence and relatedness, and the main obstacle mentioned. Select a card, or Open department →, for more detail.

The department-level view

The department view shows the department’s tiles and its own AI summary. In place of names, it has an Engagement at a glance block with counts only:

  • how many have not set any goals this month
  • how many have not written a Friday reflection
  • how many mention stress or low energy

A note at the bottom reminds you that individual goals and reflections are visible only to the department’s leader. Use the breadcrumb Organization to return.

Interpreting organizational data

The CEO never sees individual names, avatars, personal cards, goals, reflections, WOOP answers, history or leader notes – only aggregates. Use these insights to think about organizational barriers, resource allocation and where broader support could help Intended practice.

Department figures must not be used to rank departments or evaluate their leaders. The same limits as for the leader summary apply: signals are preliminary and keyword-based in the prototype.

In small departments, even counts can point to identifiable people – “1 mentions stress” in a team of four may be easy to guess. A real implementation should address this, for example with minimum group sizes before figures are shown Future development.

Additional CEO features

  • Organization tab – read all updates and write the monthly CEO update (section 7). The CEO has no Team tab.
  • Editing the Info section – as administrator, the CEO can edit the Info content directly.

Editing the Info section

  1. As CEO, open the Info tab. A chip confirms Admin: you can edit this page.
  2. Select Edit next to a section.
  3. Change the text using simple markup: ## for a subheading, - for a bullet, Q: for an FAQ question, > for a highlighted line, **text** for bold, and a blank line for a new paragraph.
  4. Select Save.

In the demo, edits are stored in your browser only, and resetting the demo restores the original text.

7
All roles

Organization – monthly updates

The Organization tab collects a monthly update from each department and from the CEO. It helps everyone see what colleagues across the organization are working on, how departments depend on each other and how individual contributions add up to something shared.

Browsing and reading updates

  1. Open the Organization tab. The latest CEO update is pinned at the top under From the CEO, followed by the department updates.
  2. Use the filter chips – All, CEO, Product, Design, Engineering, People & Culture – to narrow the list.
  3. Each post shows the department, author, month, title and a preview. Select Read more → to open the full text, and Show less to collapse it.
  4. Select Bravo! to show your appreciation. The button changes to You sent a Bravo!. No counts are shown and there is no comment section.

The demo contains five posts for November 2026, all built around the same story of improving customer onboarding: Product (Turning customer insights into meaningful improvements), Design (Making the complex a little simpler), Engineering (Building a stronger foundation for what comes next), People & Culture (Creating better conditions for people to do their work) and the CEO (Different contributions, shared momentum).

Writing an update

Leaders write for their own department with Write monthly update; the CEO uses Write CEO update. Both buttons sit at the top of the Organization tab.

  1. Select the gold write button.
  2. Read the guidance at the top of the editor.
  3. Add a Title and write the Update, starting a new line for each paragraph.
  4. Select Save draft to continue later, or Publish to share it. A title is required to publish.

Drafts appear under Your drafts (visible only to you) with a Continue button. Publishing notifies everyone in the organization through the bell. Your own published posts are marked Your update and can still be changed with Edit.

What makes a good update

Department update

  • What the department has worked on
  • How members have contributed collectively
  • What you achieved, learned or developed
  • Challenges and adjustments along the way
  • Collaboration with other departments
  • How the work contributes to the wider organization

CEO update

  • Connects the departments into one story
  • Shows how departments depend on and enable each other
  • Recognizes collective development and learning
  • Reminds everyone they contribute to something together
  • Avoids creating performance pressure

Focus on learning, contributions and collaboration – including less visible work such as knowledge sharing, experimentation and helping others. Describe progress compared with where you were, not with other teams, and avoid rankings or “best” and “top” language. Updates must never identify or evaluate individuals, or include anything from personal goals and reflections. Not every month has to be a success story: honest accounts of challenges and learning are just as valuable Intended practice.

Our momentum is something we create together.

9
Leaders

Leader Handbook

The Leader Handbook is an evidence-informed leadership development resource built into momentum. It explains how everyday leadership behaviour shapes employees’ motivation, their basic psychological needs and the motivational climate in a department. Its starting point is simple: the same application can support autonomous motivation in one department and create pressure in another, depending on how leaders use it.

Opening the handbook

  1. Switch to the Leader role.
  2. Open the Info tab.
  3. Select the gold Leader Handbook button in the purple banner.

The handbook opens as a book covering about 80% of the screen, with a page-turn animation. Close it with Esc, the × button or by clicking outside the book. When you open it again, it returns to the page you were on.

Finding your way around

The handbook has eight pages: the cover with contents, six chapters and the Leadership Reflection Tool. The indicator at the top shows where you are, for example Cover, Chapter 3 of 6 or Reflection Tool. You can move around in several ways:

Turn pages

The gold arrow buttons, the ← and → keys, or swiping left and right on a touch screen.

Jump

Choose a chapter in the contents, use the Contents link at the foot of every page, or Next chapter at the end of a chapter.

On desktop, each chapter is a two-page spread. The left page shows the chapter number, title and an In this chapter list of clickable section links. The right page holds the text, which you scroll; the chapter name stays at the top with a gold bar showing how far you have read, and a small arrow at the bottom tells you there is more below.

On mobile, the handbook shows one page at a time, with the chapter title at the top of the text. On small phones, the arrow buttons move below the book.

What the chapters cover

ChapterIn short
1 · Your role as a leaderYour influence on motivation; autonomous versus controlled reasons for working; support, not evaluation; discretion with what employees share.
2 · Supporting the three psychological needsPractical ways to support autonomy, competence and relatedness – with questions to ask. Autonomy is not the same as independence.
3 · Creating a mastery-oriented cultureHow what you recognize shapes the climate; responding to mistakes and unfinished goals with curiosity; leading by example.
4 · Supporting goals and reflectionsUsing goals, WOOP and reflections without taking over; internal versus organizational obstacles; turning insights into action. Ends with an example of a controlling and a supportive response to Kari’s reflection.
5 · The art of motivating feedbackInformational rather than controlling feedback; listening first; being specific; the Understand – Acknowledge – Explore – Support approach.
6 · Building shared momentumMutual support, connecting work to the bigger picture, writing department updates, warning signs that momentum is becoming counterproductive, and developing your own leadership.

The Leadership Reflection Tool

The last page asks How have I supported my people this month? It contains ten statements grouped under Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness, Motivational climate, Support and Leadership development, followed by two open questions: What have I learned about my leadership this month? and What is one aspect of my leadership I would like to develop further?

  1. Tick the statements that describe areas you feel you have actively supported. There is no expectation to tick every box.
  2. Answer the two open questions in your own words.
  3. Select Copy my reflection. Your ticked statements and answers are copied to the clipboard, ready to paste into your own notes.
  4. Next month, select Reset (it appears after copying) and confirm with Clear to start afresh.

Your entries are saved in your browser between visits. The tool gives no score, ranking or evaluation; it is for your own development. The handbook encourages leaders to set a development goal for their own leadership, but there is currently no separate goal-setting Dashboard or WOOP feature for leaders in the application.

10
Everyday use

Recommended rhythm

momentum works best as a small, regular part of the working week rather than something you check all the time. Set aside some time at the beginning and end of each week to thoughtfully set your goals and reflect on your progress; in between, use it whenever you find it valuable Intended practice.

Start of the month
EmployeeSet one meaningful monthly goal and work through WOOP.
LeaderBe available to talk goals through; help people find the right level of challenge without taking over.
CEOLook at organization-wide patterns from the past month.
Start of the week
EmployeeSet two specific, meaningful and realistic weekly goals; link them to the monthly goal if it makes sense.
LeaderGlance at the Dashboard and the AI summary; clarify priorities where needed.
CEO–
During the week
EmployeeTick off achieved goals, adjust goals if circumstances change, send a Bravo! when you feel like it.
LeaderFollow up on barriers you can remove; use 1:1 notes to prepare conversations.
CEO–
Friday
EmployeeWrite your reflection in your own words and save it.
LeaderRead reflections with an open mind; note what to follow up in everyday conversations.
CEORead the weekly organization summary for common barriers.
Once a month
EmployeeRead updates from other departments and the CEO.
LeaderWrite the department update; complete the Leadership Reflection Tool.
CEOWrite the CEO update connecting all departments.
Use it in a way that supports your work rather than interrupts it.

Investing real thought in goals and reflections is what makes them valuable – but momentum should never feel like an extra obligation. If it starts to, that is worth raising: adjust your goals, change how you use the app or talk to your leader.

11
Trust

Privacy and responsible use

Clear rules about who sees what are central to momentum. Employees should be able to set meaningful goals and reflect honestly without worrying about being evaluated. The table shows the intended access model.

InformationEmployee (own)ColleaguesOwn leaderCEO
Name and avatar✓✓✓Not in insights
That a goal was achieved✓✓ (goal 1, 2 or monthly)✓Counts only
Goal content✓—✓—
WOOP reflection✓—✓—
Friday reflection✓—✓—
Coded themes and signals——✓Aggregated
Weekly history chart——✓—
Private 1:1 notes——Leader’s own—
Bravo! counts————
Monthly updates✓✓✓✓

An earlier version let employees choose whether their leader could see their goals. In the current version, leader access is always on: employees cannot switch it off. The purpose is support – a basis for meaningful conversations and individual help – and the information must not be used for performance evaluations, rankings, compensation decisions or sanctions Intended practice.

Support, not evaluation.

The intended model versus the demo

What the demo shows

The visibility rules above are reflected in what each role’s interface displays In the demo. But anyone can switch roles, there is no login or server-side access control, and all data sits in the visitor’s browser. The prototype is not a secure employee data platform and must not hold real or confidential information.

What a live version needs

Real authentication and role-based access control, secure server-side storage, data retention and deletion rules, and privacy arrangements that meet data protection law (such as the GDPR) Future development.

Responsible use – for everyone

  • Employees keep ownership of their goals, share what they are comfortable sharing and adjust goals when circumstances change.
  • Leaders use insights to support, not to monitor, compare or judge – and treat what employees share with discretion.
  • Senior leadership treats aggregates as signals about working conditions, not as rankings of departments or leaders.
  • Everyone remembers that structural barriers – workload, resources, unclear expectations – are an organizational responsibility, not individual shortcomings.
12
Help

Troubleshooting and technical FAQ

What should I do if recent changes are not showing?

First, refresh the page (F5 or Ctrl+R, Cmd+R on Mac). If the site itself has been updated and you still see an older version, do a hard refresh (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R on Mac). A hard refresh reloads the website without using the browser’s cached copy.

Neither a refresh nor a hard refresh deletes your demo data – your goals, reflections and other changes stay in the browser. Only Reset demo data, or clearing the browser’s site data, removes them.

Why is my information different in another browser or device?

The prototype stores your changes in the local storage of the browser you are using. Nothing is sent to a server, so another browser, another device or another visitor starts from the original demo data. Private or incognito windows also start fresh, and forget your changes when you close them.

What happens when I reset the demo?

Everything returns to the original demonstration state, immediately and without a confirmation step: goals, reflections, WOOP plans, 1:1 notes, drafts and published updates, avatars, Info edits and Leadership Reflection Tool entries. The first-visit role hint also returns. This cannot be undone.

Why are there no actual push notifications?

The prototype has no server, so it cannot send notifications to your phone or email. Notifications appear only inside the application, under the bell. A real implementation could add push or email notifications, designed to support engagement without creating pressure to check in constantly.

Is the AI summary generated by a real AI model?

No. In the prototype, reflections are coded with keyword rules and the summary is built from that coding, as the small print on the summary card explains. A future implementation could use an AI model for more nuanced analysis. In either case, the summary is a starting point for conversation, not a psychological assessment or a validated measure of motivation.

Can I use real confidential employee information in the demo?

No. The demo has no login, anyone using the same browser can switch roles and see everything, and data is not protected. Use only the demonstration data or invented examples.

I can’t tick off a goal or choose a monthly stage.

Write the goal first. momentum asks you to enter a weekly goal before marking it achieved, and a monthly goal before choosing a progress stage.

I can’t find the Team tab or the Leader Handbook.

Check which role you are viewing as (the label next to the bell on desktop, or the avatar menu). The CEO role has no Team tab, and the Leader Handbook button appears on the Info tab only in the Leader role.

“Copy my reflection” doesn’t work.

Some browsers block clipboard access. If momentum shows “Copy is not available in this browser”, select and copy your answers manually, or try another browser.

The week number or month looks wrong.

The prototype takes the week and month from your device’s date and time settings. Check that they are correct.

The “Try the different roles!” hint has disappeared.

It is shown until you close it or open the avatar menu. Reset the demo data to see it again – or simply open the avatar menu and use Demo · view as.
